# Helheimr: canonical, contested, and the false forms on record

This name carries no diacritics to lose: **Helheimr** is complete exactly as the keyboard writes it. The register's work here is subtler — defending the *spelling* against the respellings.

## At a Glance

- **Canonical form:** Helheimr
- **Original script:** ᚼᛁᛚᚼᛁᛘᚱ
- **Pantheon:** Norse
- **Convention:** normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them
- **False forms on record:** 0
- **Contested forms:** none attested
- **Series:** The Canonical Register, No. 97 of 271

## The Canonical Form

The attested form is **ᚼᛁᛚᚼᛁᛘᚱ**, from the tradition's own record. The canonical transliteration is **Helheimr**.

No diacritics are required here: the canonical form is the exactness of the spelling itself, the form normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them demands.

## Where the Flattened Form Stands

The plain form *helheimr* differs from the canonical **Helheimr** only by convention of display — case, not content. It is **acceptable everywhere**: in legacy systems, in plain-text citation, in the DNS itself. What is not acceptable is what follows in the register: respellings that change the letters, not just their case.

## The Register of False Forms

No circulating form of this name currently qualifies as false under the register's standard — a rare standing. The spelling is short, sturdy, and rarely mangled. The forms that *do* vary from the canonical are handled below: the flattened form (already ruled acceptable) and any contested variants with real support.

## The Contested Forms

No alternate form of this name carries documented scholarly support in the lexicon's record. The convention here — normalized Old Norse spelling — þ, ð, ǫ, æ and length marks preserved as the editions print them — produces exactly one defensible transliteration: **Helheimr**. Forms that differ from it are not contested; they are simply wrong.

## What the Address Bar Allows

IDNA 2008 permits the letters these restorations use — macrons, acutes, underdots, thorn, ogonek, the lot — and the DNS carries them as punycode (`xn--` labels). Two honest constraints remain. First, **registrar inventory**: the protocol permits a character; the registrar's stock decides whether the exact domain can be bought today. Second, **combined marks**: forms like *Apṓllōn* (acute stacked on a macron) are philologically ideal yet effectively untypeable on phones and unsupported across much of the registration system.

That is why the rulebook keeps a fallback hierarchy — full restoration first, then the circumflex when the source carries one, then the macron-only academic standard, then an attested variant, and only as a last resort the plain ASCII form. **Every step down the ladder is still defensible; nothing on the ladder is a wrong mark.** A fallback is a choice among attested forms. A false form is not on the ladder at all.

## The Verdict

**Helheimr** is the canonical form: attested, checkable, and enforced across the temple, the lexicon, the cards, the APIs, and this register. The plain form *helheimr* shares that standing — the two are the same name in every system. The false forms above are documented so that no reader has to take the temple's word on faith — the violations are stated, the sources are named, and the register stands open to challenge on every line.

The temple of **Helheimr** stands at [/sites/helheimr/](/sites/helheimr/).
